blocks.content: Every algorithm covered so far in this module, from first come first served through priority scheduling, is a clean textbook idea that isolates one lesson at a time. Real production operating systems do not run any single one of these in its pure form. Linux and Windows use sophisticated hybrids, refined over decades against real, messy workloads, that borrow ideas from several algorithms at once. This chapter surveys what actually runs inside a modern operating system today.

This chapter walks through multilevel queue scheduling and the rigid limitation that eventually forced it to evolve, the multilevel feedback queue that fixed that limitation by letting processes move between queues based on their behavior, the Completely Fair Scheduler that modern Linux actually uses today, a brief look at how Windows approaches the same problem, and finally how to talk about all of this confidently in an interview.
1. Multilevel Queue Scheduling

Multilevel queue scheduling starts from a simple observation: not every process behaves the same way, so not every process should be scheduled the same way. Instead of one ready queue holding every process, the ready queue is split into several separate queues, grouped by process type or priority level. A typical split might put interactive, foreground processes, the kind a user is actively waiting on, into one queue, and batch or background processes, the kind that quietly grind through work with no one watching, into another. Each queue can then run its own scheduling algorithm, chosen to suit what that category of process actually needs.

blocks.title: A concrete layout
blocks.content: A foreground queue might use round robin with a short time quantum, so interactive processes get quick, frequent turns and the system feels responsive. A background queue might use plain first come first served, since batch jobs are not in a hurry and simplicity is enough.

Splitting processes into queues only solves half the problem. The queues themselves also need to be scheduled relative to each other, since the processor can only run one process at a time regardless of which queue it came from. Real systems handle this in one of two ways.

["Strict priority between queues: the higher priority queue is always drained completely before the scheduler even looks at a lower priority queue. A low priority queue only gets to run once every higher queue is empty.","Fixed ratio time slicing between queues: the processor is split between queues by a fixed percentage, for example eighty percent of CPU time to the foreground queue and twenty percent to the background queue, regardless of how many processes are waiting in each."]
items: Strict priority between queues: the higher priority queue is always drained completely before the scheduler even looks at a lower priority queue. A low priority queue only gets to run once every higher queue is empty.

Fixed ratio time slicing between queues: the processor is split between queues by a fixed percentage, for example eighty percent of CPU time to the foreground queue and twenty percent to the background queue, regardless of how many processes are waiting in each.

blocks.content: 2. The Key Limitation of Multilevel Queue Scheduling
blocks.text: 2. The Key Limitation of Multilevel Queue Scheduling

blocks.content: Multilevel queue scheduling has one significant weakness: a process is normally assigned to a queue once, when it is created, and it stays in that queue for its entire lifetime. That assignment is rigid. Consider a batch job that starts out purely CPU bound, crunching numbers with no user waiting on it, but later begins waiting on frequent, small chunks of interactive input, perhaps because it now feeds a live dashboard. Its behavior has genuinely changed, it now looks like an interactive process, but pure multilevel queue scheduling has no mechanism to move it into a more suitable queue. It stays stuck in the batch queue, competing for CPU time on the batch queue's terms, no matter how interactive it becomes.

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: A scheduling policy that cannot adapt to how a process actually behaves will eventually schedule some processes badly. Fixed categories were an early attempt at real world scheduling, but real workloads do not stay in one category forever.
3. Multilevel Feedback Queue Scheduling

The multilevel feedback queue is the practical fix for exactly this rigidity. It keeps the idea of several queues, typically ordered from highest priority with the shortest time quantum down to lowest priority with the longest time quantum, but it adds one crucial capability: processes can move between queues over time, based on how they actually behave, instead of being locked into a single queue forever.

The rule for moving down is straightforward. A process that repeatedly uses its entire time quantum without voluntarily giving up the CPU is behaving like a CPU bound batch job. Each time this happens, the scheduler demotes it to a lower priority queue, one with a longer time quantum, since a CPU bound job does not need fast turnaround as much as it needs long, uninterrupted stretches of processor time.

The rule for moving up, or simply staying near the top, works in the opposite direction. A process that frequently gives up the CPU early, before its quantum expires, because it is waiting on input or output, is behaving like an interactive job. That kind of process is promoted to, or kept in, a higher priority queue with a shorter time quantum, so it gets fast, frequent turns and the system stays responsive to it.

The multilevel feedback queue does not need to know in advance whether a process is interactive or CPU bound. It watches how the process actually behaves and adjusts, which is what makes it self tuning.

This adaptive, self tuning behavior, rewarding processes that behave interactively and gradually demoting processes that behave like batch jobs, without ever needing to know a process's true nature in advance, is exactly why the multilevel feedback queue became the practical foundation underneath most real world schedulers, including the Linux schedulers that came before the one it uses today.
4. The Completely Fair Scheduler in Linux
blocks.text: 4. The Completely Fair Scheduler in Linux

blocks.content: Modern Linux does not schedule processes with fixed time quantums and queues the way a multilevel feedback queue does. Since kernel version 2.6.23, its default scheduler has been the Completely Fair Scheduler, usually shortened to CFS, and it approaches fairness from a genuinely different angle.

Instead of handing out a fixed size time quantum, CFS tracks a running number for every process called its virtual runtime, often abbreviated vruntime. Virtual runtime is roughly how much CPU time a process has already received, weighted by its priority, which in Linux is expressed as a nice value. A process with a more favorable nice value accumulates virtual runtime more slowly for the same amount of real CPU time, so it is effectively treated as though it used less. Whenever the scheduler has to pick the next process to run, it simply picks whichever runnable process has the least virtual runtime so far.

blocks.title: Why it is called completely fair
blocks.content: Always picking the process with the least accumulated, weight adjusted CPU time means that over any stretch of time, every process ends up receiving CPU time in proportion to its assigned weight. No process can be starved indefinitely and no process can hog the processor, which is the fairness guarantee the name promises.

Finding the runnable process with the smallest virtual runtime quickly, out of possibly thousands of processes, is itself a data structure problem. CFS keeps runnable processes in a red black tree, ordered by virtual runtime, so the process with the least virtual runtime always sits at the leftmost node, and inserting a process that just ran back into the tree at its new virtual runtime is a fast, logarithmic time operation. It is a nice, concrete example of a self balancing binary search tree solving a real scheduling problem, not just a textbook data structures exercise.
5. Windows Scheduler, Briefly

Windows takes a different approach from modern Linux, though the underlying spirit is familiar. Its scheduler is priority based and preemptive, organized in a way that is conceptually similar to a multilevel feedback queue: threads sit at different priority levels, and the scheduler always tries to run the highest priority runnable thread. Windows adds dynamic priority boosting on top of this, temporarily raising the priority of interactive processes and of threads that have just been unblocked after waiting, such as one that just received the keyboard input or disk data it was waiting on, so the system stays responsive to whatever the user is doing right now. The full implementation has many more moving parts, but the deep details sit outside what this course needs. What matters here is the family resemblance: priority levels, preemption, and dynamic adjustment based on observed behavior, the same ingredients as a multilevel feedback queue, applied by a different operating system.

7. Why Real Schedulers Had to Evolve Beyond the Textbook
blocks.text: 7. Why Real Schedulers Had to Evolve Beyond the Textbook

blocks.content: Textbook scheduling algorithms are deliberately simple because each one is meant to teach a single idea in isolation. Shortest job first teaches you the value of knowing burst length. Priority scheduling teaches you the value of importance and the danger of starvation. Real workloads on a real machine do not arrive so neatly labeled. A single running system might have a video call needing instant, frequent attention, a compiler chewing through a long CPU bound build, a background sync process quietly uploading files, and a dozen other processes of every shape in between, all runnable at the same moment. A good production scheduler has to handle this wildly heterogeneous mix well, and it has to keep handling it well as each process's behavior shifts over time. No single simple textbook algorithm, applied on its own, does that. That gap is exactly why multilevel feedback queues, and later designs like the Completely Fair Scheduler, exist.
8. Common Mistakes and the Interview Angle
blocks.text: 8. Common Mistakes and the Interview Angle

blocks.content: Common mistakes

["Assuming Linux literally uses Round Robin: older, simpler Unix schedulers leaned on ideas like this, but the scheduler in a modern Linux kernel is CFS, a genuinely different design built around virtual runtime, not fixed time quantums.","Assuming Linux literally uses Priority Scheduling in its pure textbook form: nice values do influence scheduling under CFS, but they act as weights on virtual runtime accumulation, not as a simple always run the highest priority process rule.","Treating multilevel queue and multilevel feedback queue as the same thing: the defining feature of the feedback version is that processes can move between queues. Without that movement, it is just multilevel queue scheduling with its permanent assignment limitation."]
items: Assuming Linux literally uses Round Robin: older, simpler Unix schedulers leaned on ideas like this, but the scheduler in a modern Linux kernel is CFS, a genuinely different design built around virtual runtime, not fixed time quantums.

Assuming Linux literally uses Priority Scheduling in its pure textbook form: nice values do influence scheduling under CFS, but they act as weights on virtual runtime accumulation, not as a simple always run the highest priority process rule.

Treating multilevel queue and multilevel feedback queue as the same thing: the defining feature of the feedback version is that processes can move between queues. Without that movement, it is just multilevel queue scheduling with its permanent assignment limitation.

blocks.content: The interview angle

When an interviewer asks how Linux actually schedules processes, naming the Completely Fair Scheduler specifically, and being able to describe virtual runtime at a high level, that the scheduler always favors whichever runnable process has received the least weighted CPU time so far, is a strong signal. It shows you know the difference between the clean textbook algorithms used to teach the underlying tradeoffs and the adaptive, hybrid systems that actually run in production, which is precisely the gap this chapter is meant to close.
